title: The Monkey's Paw: inference and evidence
prompt: Read the excerpt, then choose the best answer for each question.

items.stem: When Mr. White asks about the monkey's paw, Morris answers "hastily": "Nothing. Leastways nothing worth hearing." What does his reaction suggest?

choices.text: He wants to sell the paw to Mr. White
choices.misconception: takes his later, abandoned idea of selling it as his aim here

choices.text: He is uneasy about the paw and would rather not discuss it
The paw really is a worthless trinket
choices.misconception: accepts "nothing worth hearing" at face value, missing his evasion

choices.text: He has forgotten the story
choices.misconception: ignores that he answers "hastily" to avoid the topic

items.stem: Which detail most strongly supports the inference that Morris regrets using his own wishes?

choices.text: "It had a spell put on it by an old fakir," said the sergeant-major.
choices.misconception: cites a fact about the spell, not Morris's feelings about wishing

choices.text: "Sounds like the Arabian Nights," said Mrs. White.
choices.misconception: cites Mrs. White's joke, which shows nothing about Morris

choices.text: "I have," he said, quietly, and his blotchy face whitened.
His host filled it for him.
choices.misconception: cites a host's courtesy that says nothing about regret

items.stem: According to Morris, why did the fakir put a spell on the paw?

choices.text: To make three men rich
choices.misconception: adds a purpose that Morris never states

choices.text: To protect soldiers serving in India
choices.misconception: ties the spell to Morris's army service, which the text never does

choices.text: To show that fate rules people's lives and that those who interfere with it are sorry
To punish Morris for a crime
choices.misconception: invents a crime; the text gives no reason to punish Morris

items.stem: Morris says the first owner's third wish "was for death." What can you infer from this?

choices.text: The first owner wished for Morris to die
choices.misconception: invents a target; the text says only "for death"

choices.text: Morris made that wish himself
choices.misconception: overlooks that the wish belonged to "the first man"

choices.text: The paw grants only happy wishes
choices.misconception: contradicts "It has caused enough mischief already"

choices.text: The first owner's earlier wishes probably brought him misery

items.stem: Why does Morris say people won't buy the paw?

choices.text: Some think it is a fairy tale, and others want to try it before paying
It costs too much
choices.misconception: gives a reason with no support in Morris's words

choices.text: All of its wishes are used up
choices.misconception: takes the reason from Mr. White's remark, not Morris's answer

choices.text: It is too ugly to sell
choices.misconception: infers a reason from Mrs. White's grimace instead of Morris's words

items.stem: What can the reader infer from Morris throwing the paw onto the fire?

choices.text: He believes the paw is dangerous and wants it destroyed
He is angry at Mr. White for asking questions
choices.misconception: infers anger that no detail in the text supports

choices.text: He dropped it by accident
choices.misconception: overlooks that he "suddenly threw it" and says "Better let it burn"

choices.text: He wants to prove the paw cannot burn
choices.misconception: invents a test, though he tells White to let it burn

items.stem: Which detail most strongly supports the inference that Morris thinks the paw is dangerous?

choices.text: "To look at, it's just an ordinary little paw, dried to a mummy."
choices.misconception: cites its plain look, which suggests no danger

choices.text: "I did have some idea of selling it."
choices.misconception: cites a plan to sell it, weak evidence of danger

choices.text: "Sounds like the Arabian Nights," said Mrs. White.
choices.misconception: cites Mrs. White's joke, not Morris's view

choices.text: "It has caused enough mischief already."

items.stem: How does Mrs. White react when Morris first holds out the paw?

choices.text: She takes it eagerly
choices.misconception: gives Herbert's curiosity to Mrs. White

choices.text: She asks to make a wish
choices.misconception: moves her later joke about four pairs of hands to this moment

choices.text: She draws back with a grimace
She laughs at Morris
choices.misconception: moves the family's later laughter to this moment

items.stem: What can you infer about Mr. White from how he handles the paw across the excerpt?

choices.text: He grows more eager to own and use it despite every warning
He is afraid of the paw
choices.misconception: overlooks that he snatches it from the fire and asks how

choices.text: He wants to destroy it
choices.misconception: gives Morris's wish to burn the paw to Mr. White

choices.text: He does not care about it
choices.misconception: ignores that he examined "his new possession closely"

items.stem: Which detail most strongly shows that the Whites do not take Morris's warning seriously?

choices.text: His hearers felt their light laughter "jarred somewhat."
choices.misconception: picks the moment the family briefly does take Morris seriously

choices.text: All three burst into laughter as Mr. White takes out the paw
Mrs. White drew back with a grimace.
choices.misconception: reads disgust at the paw as disbelief in the warning

choices.text: "Hold it up in your right hand and wish aloud," said the sergeant-major.
choices.misconception: cites Morris's instructions, which show nothing about the family
